Pembury Lifestyle Group - Piercing the corporate Veil of PLG

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
An exclusive expose on how the CEO of PLG is breaching laws and ripping off shareholders

Unique Selling Point:
Exclusive material on a private conversation that has been recorded

Summary:
In early December of 2019, two men met at the BOSSA café close to Northcliff, for coffee. Andrew McLachlan, CEO of Pembury lifestyle group, and the chairman of his board Martin Nel. Their conversation was around the future of the business, a company exposed by Carte Blanche six months before this conversation took place

Andrew McLachlan “I do not want to stay on as a listed company.”

These two had been friends for 30 years, but the friendship would soon end, because the chairman was secretly taping his CEO’s every word, and what McLachlan said about his own company was both startling and in breach of the companies act:

“PLG IS GONE. I AM TAKING THE SHIP INTO THE HARBOUR AND I AM BOMBING IT.”



Further information:
Andrew McLachlan was founder of the PLG group of schools that promised affordable, quality private school education. In 2017 he listed PLG on the JSE, and promised their shareholders – many of them teachers and parents, the world. Three years later for every R100 they invested they are lucky to get a return of R5 and even he managed a nod at their losses. I feel sorry for the investors he told Martin that day, but his pity was momentary.

“We are not working with PLG schools that we are burying as deep as we can into the earth,” he said.

One of the investors is the Black management forum investment company or BFMI. They believed in Andrew once, and invested R56 million. Three years later they are fuming. Not only at the loss of their investment down to about R3 million, but at what they call Andrew’s machinations. These include a wide range of breaches of corporate governance from disrespecting directors to all out fraud. Bheki Sibiya is the chairperson of BFMI

Bheki Sibiya
The issue of muddling up messing up the corporate governance, it is Andrew’s way of wanting to steal the company, and he is on record as saying he wants to cause quite a bit of mess so he buys the minorities cheaply and then delists the company

Sibiya has lost faith with the JSE who he says knows about all of this and has done absolutely nothing.

“We are dealing with the issue of JSE as being a toothless bulldog. They are useless! They see these as shareholder issues, but when you have a shareholder that is suppressing minority rights, in my view the minimum that JSE should be doing is censuring the majority shareholder but JSE is toothless.”

Editor of the Financial Mail Rob Rose agrees and in February wrote a piece on PLG in which he likened the shenanigans on the board to the Wild West. Other former directors say it’s like a Tarantino movie and its easy to agree with that assessment. Late last year the directors managed to get Andrew McLachlan suspended, but using bouncers and thuggish tactics he has so far prevailed. Several financial directors have resigned suddenly, the company secretary Arbor Capital is gone, and the former auditors who raised the red flag on accounting irregularities were let go, without being paid, and have now applied to court to liquidate the company. They are not the only ones, Mark Liquorish from Abacus who will go on camera, has also applied to liquidate PLG. McLachlan tried to make a deal and offered them one of the few properties he owns as security until he had paid them what he owed them. That sounded good until ABACUS spoke to the former auditors who have also applied for their liquidation and found out that Andrew M had offered them the same property as collateral. Disgusted they are both marching off to court to take on PLG.

Meanwhile Andrew is trying to squeeze as much as he can out of the company and asked the board members to come back in the middle of the December holidays to vote on raising his salary to R500 000 per month. He hoped he could raise enough capital on that salary to pay out the minority shareholders around R20 million rand if he delists the company.
At the last minute the meeting was cancelled.

Imagine if as a teacher you had put in some of your hard- earned savings, your investment tanked and now you find that Andrew M is funneling the money that PLG is making into his wife’s account?
“And they are now changing the accounts so that whosoever pays PLG think they are paying PLG but the money gets into his wife’s company” says Bheki Sibiya.

But why would Andrew do that? It’s simple and he explained all of it, except the fraudulent bits to Martin Nel over coffee that day. ( But we have someone close to one of the other directors who can fill in the bits on the Fraud and the TERS funds – although she wants her identity hidden.)

Andrew spelled out his cunning plans to the Chairperson of the board in some detail about how he plans to delist and start another company doing basically the same thing – opening schools and making a fortune. But the only people who have made a fortune out of PLG is Andrew McLachlan and his family including his son Jason who is a board member and dallying around in a company starting schools called ACE.

When Carte Blanche first exposed PLG it was evident they weren’t paying their bills, and nothing much seems to have changed, so is PLG short of cash? It appears so, but Andrew was happy to brag about his wealth and how clever he has been to his chairperson. He told him how he is interested in buying Four Ways Mall which we have established is valued at around ??, and he also boasted that he will end up with R140 million in paid up properties.

That fact may not sit that well with his teaching staff who have had their salaries cut in half, and some of his former staff who he retrenched at the beginning of lockdown. It may also not sit that well with the old people from Bryanston retirement village whom he turfed out in the middle of a pandemic during the lockdown, so he could begin renovations to start his new school using PLG funding.

The story will also include other voices who have been at the short end of the PLG story.

Script:


FINAL SCRIPT PLG 2020 SCHOOL’S OUT FOR TX SUNDAY 28th JUNE
Fact Checked, to length, with all legal additions and with new promo 3/2

Commentary One
Meet Andrew McLachlan founder and CEO of the Pembury lifestyle group or PLG. In 2017 he raised R140 million from investors on the JSE. They bought his promise of affordable quality private school education. Three years later they’ve lost most of their money

Bheki Sibiya
This is the worst performing investment that BMFI has done in its 25 years of existence, worst by far!

Commentary two
Meet Bheki Sibiya - chairperson of the Black management forum investment company that holds 15% of PLG shares- excited by the growth in private school education they sunk R55 million rand into the company
Derek
What is that investment worth today?
Bheki
It’s worth about R4.9 million rand so it’s decimated a huge amount of shareholder value

Commentary Three
McLachlan is not a popular man here at BMFI, they have called him out on a range of governance breaches. then barred Sibiya and his predecessor from board meetings. McLachlan denies any breaches of the Companies Act and says no duly appointed directors have ever been barred from attending meetings.

Bheki Sibiya
I am hating to say it, but you may find Andrew is to PLG, what Jacob Zuma was to the country

Commentary Four
PLG had 11 schools in its portfolio, then McLachlan added several retirement villages, but complaints about the schools soon reached Carte Blanche. Former headmaster of PLG Mellow Oaks, Andrew Stewart

Andy Stewart Carte Blanche June 2019
For me it’s a company that just neglects, abuses..

Commentary Five
The schools were run down, and the quality of education at some of them wasn’t
up to scratch. Our own investigation in June 2019 exposed how they were also defaulting on their leases of the school properties.

Andrew Stewart CB June 2019
I would suggest there is a huge level of ineptitude and incompetence, but the driving factor as far as I can see it, is greed.


Commentary Six
Greed was a prominent theme of our previous story, and it’s the hallmark of this one, with all fingers pointing to Andrew McLachlan as the CEO of PLG.

Malyssa Hattingh
They have preyed on the most vulnerable segments of any society, being children and the elderly, and I don’t know how they sleep at night

Commentary Seven
This is Allen’s View school which has since closed down, before that Aiden Hattingh was a learner there. We met his mother Malyssa at the Rand club where she works. After our story in June last year, she was worried- we had exposed how the Randfontein school was not registered with the department-

So Malyssa did her own investigation and confirmed her worst fears. Her son’ Aiden’s school wasn’t registered either, which meant his school year wouldn’t be recognised

Malyssa
I don’t think I have ever felt such rage. It’s one thing not to apply for registration, but to lie to take our money

Commentary eight
Malyssa has laid criminal charges against McLachlan and some directors, and she gave us the case number. McLachlan says he knows nothing of these charges and that all the required documents for Allen’s View were submitted to the GDE.

Derek
Malyssa in your view what should happen to Andrew McLachlan
Malyssa
Andrew needs to go to jail, he committed fraud. This is white collar crime

Commentary nine
Malyssa is one of many to cry foul. There is trouble at the top of the organisation as well.
Just before the new year, PLG’s chairperson, Martin Nel met with Andrew McLachlan for coffee.

Derek Link
These two men had been friends for 30 years, but their friendship would soon end, because the chairman was secretly taping his CEO’s every word, and what Andrew McLachlan was saying about his own company was startling, and possibly even criminal

Commentary Ten
This recording of the actual conversation reveals that McLachlan wanted to delist from the JSE and set up a new private education company – a mirror of PLG but without the hassle of the JSE regulations.



Andrew
That’s been causing all the problems in my life. Stress, I don’t want to do IFRS, I don’t want to answer to the JSE, they actually bring the value of your company right down

Commentary eleven
As the CEO of a JSE listed company McLachlan has a fiduciary duty to protect the company and its shareholders, but instead it seems he wanted to destroy PLG.

Andrew
You know what you are never going to have a thing improve once you have got a bad name and we were suspended for seven months, then we were on Carte Blanche
Martin
Ja, but we can still turn that around
Andrew
PLG is gone. I am taking the ship into the harbour and I am bombing it.

Commentary Twelve
Not only bombing it, but burying it too

Andrew
I mean we are not working with PLG schools, that we are burying as deep as we can into the earth. It’s been called Aquarian Academies

Commentary Thirteen
McLachlan urges his chairperson to buy shares in this new company, and he plots how he can pay out as little as possible to minority shareholders like BMFI

Derek
Why would you want to destroy the company, bomb it as he puts it?
Bheki
Now he is looking at this international financial reporting standards- IFRS it is too restrictive it does not give him the latitude to do what he wants to do and that is why he says I want to bomb it. Because when that happens, he will offer people like BFMI a pittance.

Commentary fourteen
Ring Ring

We asked McLachlan for an interview. Why would he want to destroy his own company?

Derek: Andrew McLachlan isn’t answering

We went to his offices

Then he sent a letter saying this allegation makes no commercial sense as he owns almost half of PLG. He also said the board decided against delisting as it wouldn’t benefit shareholders.

McLachlan is still bitter about our first expose.

Andrew McLachlan
I can tell you now that her and the Carte Blanche executive producer will be arrested. We are hitting Multichoice and Devi with a R20 million lawsuit

Commentary Fifteen
So, McLachlan may not like this story either. Meet Anthea Ntsemi a caregiver who spent 15 years working here at PLG’s Bryanston retirement village. Her salary- a modest R4000 per month.

Anthea
I loved my job that makes me stay for a long time

Commentary sixteen
But two days before lockdown her world came crashing down. The entire staff received an SMS. Bryanston retirement lodge was closing its doors

Anthea
You can see something is fishy, but no one is telling us anything

Commentary seventeen
McLachlan signed her severance package – five tranches of her salary from April to August which still haven’t been paid. And staff were shocked when they phoned him from the Department of labour in April.

Anthea
He said to us you won’t get that money you can go to CCMA, I will meet you there. He doesn’t attend the CCMA. To me it’s like he has got no heart!

Commentary eighteen
McLachlan said they couldn’t pay because Covid19 meant the Bryanston Lodge earned nothing since March.

But It’s a common complaint, PLG doesn’t look after its staff and it doesn’t pay its bills, and its former auditors and classroom supplier have applied to liquidate the company. PLG is opposing this - it says its assets far exceed its liabilities

In December McLachlan decided he wanted a salary hike to R500 000 per month. Sibiya was one of the directors who blocked the increase

Derek
How were you treated after this?
Bheki
we were treated with disrespect, disdain and sometimes some of the directors we felt our personal security was at stake.

Commentary nineteen
And even though shareholders in PLG have lost around 90% of their money. McLachlan tells his chairperson that once he delists, he will have an entity with a portfolio of R140 million in paid up properties

Martin
Have you personally lost a lot with the listing?
Andrew
No, not much because I was very clever. I bought properties knowing they were going to double triple in value every year and they have

LINK
If you are an investor in a company, what you don’t want to hear is that revenue earned to grow that business is secretly being diverted somewhere else – and that is one of the most serious allegations emerging in this PLG saga

Commentary twenty
Meet Jason McLachlan – Andrew’s 26 year- old son and a director and shareholder of PLG. He is also the Managing director of Ace Colleges- his own brand of private schools. But its PLG money that is being funnelled to these schools, say our highly placed insiders- enriching the family at the expense of PLG shareholders

Derek
if you were to get in to Andrew McLachlan’s mind, what is his strategy?
Director
Currently his strategy would be to try and devalue the company as far as possible, and to be able to get out assets that he can, at the lowest possible rate for himself, and then uh probably close PLG down, or let it run the route where it gets either liquidated, or not.
Derek:
And then what would he do?
Director
Well he would probably carry on with a new brand, with his son's brand, the Ace brand which obviously would be direct competition of PLG.

Commentary Twenty- one
If this is the strategy, it may be a clue to why Anthea Ntsemi and her colleagues were given the boot here at Bryanston. McLachlan says he is renovating this property to become a school. Don’t bet on it being a PLG school. It is alleged that he is also diverting funds from the remaining retirement lodges

Derek
Sources tell us bank accounts have been changed to his wife's personal account and rentals have been paid by residents?


Director
Yes. The bank account that the rentals need to be paid into is his wife's bank account.
Derek
How do you regard this action?
Director
Directly that is basically theft of company assets, taking it and enriching yourself, prior to coming to any agreement

Commentary twenty- Two
McLachlan and Jason deny the allegations, calling them contrived and unsubstantiated. He says there is due process in dealing with all PLG’s assets at all times and decisions are made by the board. Jason claims ACE schools target a different market to PLG.

Bheki Sibiya
My considered opinion is Andrew is involved in the classic money laundering -taking money which belongs to PLG, channelling it to his family treasure, as it were, cos it is fraudulent, it is illegal, it's unethical.

Commentary Twenty-Three
By January, PLG’s boardroom was a battleground, and the board tried to suspend McLachlan. He said the suspension was illegal and ignored it. In Feb editor Rob Rose, from the Financial Mail, wrote that it was like the Wild West at Pembury

Rob Rose
I think it looks entirely like the Wild West, like a bunch of cowboys who just have no appreciation of the duties they have towards all shareholders, towards all investors.

Commentary Twenty- four
Internal documents show a raft of corporate governance concerns, that the JSE is well aware of, says Bheki Sibiya because they have been given all the evidence

Bheki Sibiya
The JSE has disappointed me deeply and for us as an organization BMFI, we are disappointed

Commentary Twenty- five
Rose says after Steinhoff, the JSE promised greater regulation. Pembury proves not much has changed

Rob Rose:
One of the reasons that companies list on the stock exchange and investors go and invest in those companies is because it's supposed to provide a high standard of security. The exchange implicitly gives its guarantee that it's going to look after the interests of you as an investor. In this case it doesn't seem to be happening at all.

Commentary Twenty- Six
In May we sent the JSE a list of questions about the governance breaches at Pembury

LINK JSE
The JSE told Carte Blanche in an email that they are engaging with PLG and those engagements are confidential, so no interview here, but could that be because they are embarrassed that their regulation of PLG, is too little too late?

Bheki Sibiya
My view is they are refusing to be accountable. And unfortunately, the recourse through JSE is not working. The recourse through the legal process is too expensive to pursue

THE END 13 minutes

PROMO ONE
Boardroom battles, a CEO’s conversation secretly taped, its all going wrong for a listed JSE company that offers affordable private school education

PROMO TWO
A JSE listed company is back in the news as boardroom battles erupt
Rob Rose
It looks entirely like the Wild West like a bunch of cowboys who just have no appreciation of the duties they have towards all shareholders

PROMO THREE
In 2019 we exposed a JSE listed company that was providing private schooling and retirement villages. Now we go back and pierce the corporate veil

mihle@combinedartists.co.za 16 September 2020 Script: FINAL SCRIPT PLG 2020 SCHOOL’S OUT FOR TX SUNDAY 28th JUNE Fact Checked, to length, with all legal additions and with new promo 3/2 Commentary One Meet Andrew McLachlan founder and CEO of the Pembury lifestyle group or PLG. In 2017 he raised R140 million from investors on the JSE. They bought his promise of affordable quality private school education. Three years later they’ve lost most of their money Bheki Sibiya This is the worst performing investment that BMFI has done in its 25 years of existence, worst by far! Commentary two Meet Bheki Sibiya - chairperson of the Black management forum investment company that holds 15% of PLG shares- excited by the growth in private school education they sunk R55 million rand into the company Derek What is that investment worth today? Bheki It’s worth about R4.9 million rand so it’s decimated a huge amount of shareholder value Commentary Three McLachlan is not a popular man here at BMFI, they have called him out on a range of governance breaches. then barred Sibiya and his predecessor from board meetings. McLachlan denies any breaches of the Companies Act and says no duly appointed directors have ever been barred from attending meetings. Bheki Sibiya I am hating to say it, but you may find Andrew is to PLG, what Jacob Zuma was to the country Commentary Four PLG had 11 schools in its portfolio, then McLachlan added several retirement villages, but complaints about the schools soon reached Carte Blanche. Former headmaster of PLG Mellow Oaks, Andrew Stewart Andy Stewart Carte Blanche June 2019 For me it’s a company that just neglects, abuses.. Commentary Five The schools were run down, and the quality of education at some of them wasn’t up to scratch. Our own investigation in June 2019 exposed how they were also defaulting on their leases of the school properties. Andrew Stewart CB June 2019 I would suggest there is a huge level of ineptitude and incompetence, but the driving factor as far as I can see it, is greed. Commentary Six Greed was a prominent theme of our previous story, and it’s the hallmark of this one, with all fingers pointing to Andrew McLachlan as the CEO of PLG. Malyssa Hattingh They have preyed on the most vulnerable segments of any society, being children and the elderly, and I don’t know how they sleep at night Commentary Seven This is Allen’s View school which has since closed down, before that Aiden Hattingh was a learner there. We met his mother Malyssa at the Rand club where she works. After our story in June last year, she was worried- we had exposed how the Randfontein school was not registered with the department- So Malyssa did her own investigation and confirmed her worst fears. Her son’ Aiden’s school wasn’t registered either, which meant his school year wouldn’t be recognised Malyssa I don’t think I have ever felt such rage. It’s one thing not to apply for registration, but to lie to take our money Commentary eight Malyssa has laid criminal charges against McLachlan and some directors, and she gave us the case number. McLachlan says he knows nothing of these charges and that all the required documents for Allen’s View were submitted to the GDE. Derek Malyssa in your view what should happen to Andrew McLachlan Malyssa Andrew needs to go to jail, he committed fraud. This is white collar crime Commentary nine Malyssa is one of many to cry foul. There is trouble at the top of the organisation as well. Just before the new year, PLG’s chairperson, Martin Nel met with Andrew McLachlan for coffee. Derek Link These two men had been friends for 30 years, but their friendship would soon end, because the chairman was secretly taping his CEO’s every word, and what Andrew McLachlan was saying about his own company was startling, and possibly even criminal Commentary Ten This recording of the actual conversation reveals that McLachlan wanted to delist from the JSE and set up a new private education company – a mirror of PLG but without the hassle of the JSE regulations. Andrew That’s been causing all the problems in my life. Stress, I don’t want to do IFRS, I don’t want to answer to the JSE, they actually bring the value of your company right down Commentary eleven As the CEO of a JSE listed company McLachlan has a fiduciary duty to protect the company and its shareholders, but instead it seems he wanted to destroy PLG. Andrew You know what you are never going to have a thing improve once you have got a bad name and we were suspended for seven months, then we were on Carte Blanche Martin Ja, but we can still turn that around Andrew PLG is gone. I am taking the ship into the harbour and I am bombing it. Commentary Twelve Not only bombing it, but burying it too Andrew I mean we are not working with PLG schools, that we are burying as deep as we can into the earth. It’s been called Aquarian Academies Commentary Thirteen McLachlan urges his chairperson to buy shares in this new company, and he plots how he can pay out as little as possible to minority shareholders like BMFI Derek Why would you want to destroy the company, bomb it as he puts it? Bheki Now he is looking at this international financial reporting standards- IFRS it is too restrictive it does not give him the latitude to do what he wants to do and that is why he says I want to bomb it. Because when that happens, he will offer people like BFMI a pittance. Commentary fourteen Ring Ring We asked McLachlan for an interview. Why would he want to destroy his own company? Derek: Andrew McLachlan isn’t answering We went to his offices Then he sent a letter saying this allegation makes no commercial sense as he owns almost half of PLG. He also said the board decided against delisting as it wouldn’t benefit shareholders. McLachlan is still bitter about our first expose. Andrew McLachlan I can tell you now that her and the Carte Blanche executive producer will be arrested. We are hitting Multichoice and Devi with a R20 million lawsuit Commentary Fifteen So, McLachlan may not like this story either. Meet Anthea Ntsemi a caregiver who spent 15 years working here at PLG’s Bryanston retirement village. Her salary- a modest R4000 per month. Anthea I loved my job that makes me stay for a long time Commentary sixteen But two days before lockdown her world came crashing down. The entire staff received an SMS. Bryanston retirement lodge was closing its doors Anthea You can see something is fishy, but no one is telling us anything Commentary seventeen McLachlan signed her severance package – five tranches of her salary from April to August which still haven’t been paid. And staff were shocked when they phoned him from the Department of labour in April. Anthea He said to us you won’t get that money you can go to CCMA, I will meet you there. He doesn’t attend the CCMA. To me it’s like he has got no heart! Commentary eighteen McLachlan said they couldn’t pay because Covid19 meant the Bryanston Lodge earned nothing since March. But It’s a common complaint, PLG doesn’t look after its staff and it doesn’t pay its bills, and its former auditors and classroom supplier have applied to liquidate the company. PLG is opposing this - it says its assets far exceed its liabilities In December McLachlan decided he wanted a salary hike to R500 000 per month. Sibiya was one of the directors who blocked the increase Derek How were you treated after this? Bheki we were treated with disrespect, disdain and sometimes some of the directors we felt our personal security was at stake. Commentary nineteen And even though shareholders in PLG have lost around 90% of their money. McLachlan tells his chairperson that once he delists, he will have an entity with a portfolio of R140 million in paid up properties Martin Have you personally lost a lot with the listing? Andrew No, not much because I was very clever. I bought properties knowing they were going to double triple in value every year and they have LINK If you are an investor in a company, what you don’t want to hear is that revenue earned to grow that business is secretly being diverted somewhere else – and that is one of the most serious allegations emerging in this PLG saga Commentary twenty Meet Jason McLachlan – Andrew’s 26 year- old son and a director and shareholder of PLG. He is also the Managing director of Ace Colleges- his own brand of private schools. But its PLG money that is being funnelled to these schools, say our highly placed insiders- enriching the family at the expense of PLG shareholders Derek if you were to get in to Andrew McLachlan’s mind, what is his strategy? Director Currently his strategy would be to try and devalue the company as far as possible, and to be able to get out assets that he can, at the lowest possible rate for himself, and then uh probably close PLG down, or let it run the route where it gets either liquidated, or not. Derek: And then what would he do? Director Well he would probably carry on with a new brand, with his son's brand, the Ace brand which obviously would be direct competition of PLG. Commentary Twenty- one If this is the strategy, it may be a clue to why Anthea Ntsemi and her colleagues were given the boot here at Bryanston. McLachlan says he is renovating this property to become a school. Don’t bet on it being a PLG school. It is alleged that he is also diverting funds from the remaining retirement lodges Derek Sources tell us bank accounts have been changed to his wife's personal account and rentals have been paid by residents? Director Yes. The bank account that the rentals need to be paid into is his wife's bank account. Derek How do you regard this action? Director Directly that is basically theft of company assets, taking it and enriching yourself, prior to coming to any agreement Commentary twenty- Two McLachlan and Jason deny the allegations, calling them contrived and unsubstantiated. He says there is due process in dealing with all PLG’s assets at all times and decisions are made by the board. Jason claims ACE schools target a different market to PLG. Bheki Sibiya My considered opinion is Andrew is involved in the classic money laundering -taking money which belongs to PLG, channelling it to his family treasure, as it were, cos it is fraudulent, it is illegal, it's unethical. Commentary Twenty-Three By January, PLG’s boardroom was a battleground, and the board tried to suspend McLachlan. He said the suspension was illegal and ignored it. In Feb editor Rob Rose, from the Financial Mail, wrote that it was like the Wild West at Pembury Rob Rose I think it looks entirely like the Wild West, like a bunch of cowboys who just have no appreciation of the duties they have towards all shareholders, towards all investors. Commentary Twenty- four Internal documents show a raft of corporate governance concerns, that the JSE is well aware of, says Bheki Sibiya because they have been given all the evidence Bheki Sibiya The JSE has disappointed me deeply and for us as an organization BMFI, we are disappointed Commentary Twenty- five Rose says after Steinhoff, the JSE promised greater regulation. Pembury proves not much has changed Rob Rose: One of the reasons that companies list on the stock exchange and investors go and invest in those companies is because it's supposed to provide a high standard of security. The exchange implicitly gives its guarantee that it's going to look after the interests of you as an investor. In this case it doesn't seem to be happening at all. Commentary Twenty- Six In May we sent the JSE a list of questions about the governance breaches at Pembury LINK JSE The JSE told Carte Blanche in an email that they are engaging with PLG and those engagements are confidential, so no interview here, but could that be because they are embarrassed that their regulation of PLG, is too little too late? Bheki Sibiya My view is they are refusing to be accountable. And unfortunately, the recourse through JSE is not working. The recourse through the legal process is too expensive to pursue THE END 13 minutes PROMO ONE Boardroom battles, a CEO’s conversation secretly taped, its all going wrong for a listed JSE company that offers affordable private school education PROMO TWO A JSE listed company is back in the news as boardroom battles erupt Rob Rose It looks entirely like the Wild West like a bunch of cowboys who just have no appreciation of the duties they have towards all shareholders PROMO THREE In 2019 we exposed a JSE listed company that was providing private schooling and retirement villages. Now we go back and pierce the corporate veil Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for Pembury Lifestyle Group - Piercing the corporate Veil of PLG (5693) Joy Summers 30 June 2020

metadata.Summary: In early December of 2019, two men met at the BOSSA café close to Northcliff, for coffee. Andrew McLachlan, CEO of Pembury lifestyle group, and the chairman of his board Martin Nel. Their conversation was around the future of the business, a company exposed by Carte Blanche six months before this conversation took place Andrew McLachlan “I do not want to stay on as a listed company.” These two had been friends for 30 years, but the friendship would soon end, because the chairman was secretly taping his CEO’s every word, and what McLachlan said about his own company was both startling and in breach of the companies act: “PLG IS GONE. I AM TAKING THE SHIP INTO THE HARBOUR AND I AM BOMBING IT.”
metadata.Further information: Andrew McLachlan was founder of the PLG group of schools that promised affordable, quality private school education. In 2017 he listed PLG on the JSE, and promised their shareholders – many of them teachers and parents, the world. Three years later for every R100 they invested they are lucky to get a return of R5 and even he managed a nod at their losses. I feel sorry for the investors he told Martin that day, but his pity was momentary. “We are not working with PLG schools that we are burying as deep as we can into the earth,” he said. One of the investors is the Black management forum investment company or BFMI. They believed in Andrew once, and invested R56 million. Three years later they are fuming. Not only at the loss of their investment down to about R3 million, but at what they call Andrew’s machinations. These include a wide range of breaches of corporate governance from disrespecting directors to all out fraud. Bheki Sibiya is the chairperson of BFMI Bheki Sibiya The issue of muddling up messing up the corporate governance, it is Andrew’s way of wanting to steal the company, and he is on record as saying he wants to cause quite a bit of mess so he buys the minorities cheaply and then delists the company Sibiya has lost faith with the JSE who he says knows about all of this and has done absolutely nothing. “We are dealing with the issue of JSE as being a toothless bulldog. They are useless! They see these as shareholder issues, but when you have a shareholder that is suppressing minority rights, in my view the minimum that JSE should be doing is censuring the majority shareholder but JSE is toothless.” Editor of the Financial Mail Rob Rose agrees and in February wrote a piece on PLG in which he likened the shenanigans on the board to the Wild West. Other former directors say it’s like a Tarantino movie and its easy to agree with that assessment. Late last year the directors managed to get Andrew McLachlan suspended, but using bouncers and thuggish tactics he has so far prevailed. Several financial directors have resigned suddenly, the company secretary Arbor Capital is gone, and the former auditors who raised the red flag on accounting irregularities were let go, without being paid, and have now applied to court to liquidate the company. They are not the only ones, Mark Liquorish from Abacus who will go on camera, has also applied to liquidate PLG. McLachlan tried to make a deal and offered them one of the few properties he owns as security until he had paid them what he owed them. That sounded good until ABACUS spoke to the former auditors who have also applied for their liquidation and found out that Andrew M had offered them the same property as collateral. Disgusted they are both marching off to court to take on PLG. Meanwhile Andrew is trying to squeeze as much as he can out of the company and asked the board members to come back in the middle of the December holidays to vote on raising his salary to R500 000 per month. He hoped he could raise enough capital on that salary to pay out the minority shareholders around R20 million rand if he delists the company. At the last minute the meeting was cancelled. Imagine if as a teacher you had put in some of your hard- earned savings, your investment tanked and now you find that Andrew M is funneling the money that PLG is making into his wife’s account? “And they are now changing the accounts so that whosoever pays PLG think they are paying PLG but the money gets into his wife’s company” says Bheki Sibiya. But why would Andrew do that? It’s simple and he explained all of it, except the fraudulent bits to Martin Nel over coffee that day. ( But we have someone close to one of the other directors who can fill in the bits on the Fraud and the TERS funds – although she wants her identity hidden.) Andrew spelled out his cunning plans to the Chairperson of the board in some detail about how he plans to delist and start another company doing basically the same thing – opening schools and making a fortune. But the only people who have made a fortune out of PLG is Andrew McLachlan and his family including his son Jason who is a board member and dallying around in a company starting schools called ACE. When Carte Blanche first exposed PLG it was evident they weren’t paying their bills, and nothing much seems to have changed, so is PLG short of cash? It appears so, but Andrew was happy to brag about his wealth and how clever he has been to his chairperson. He told him how he is interested in buying Four Ways Mall which we have established is valued at around ??, and he also boasted that he will end up with R140 million in paid up properties. That fact may not sit that well with his teaching staff who have had their salaries cut in half, and some of his former staff who he retrenched at the beginning of lockdown. It may also not sit that well with the old people from Bryanston retirement village whom he turfed out in the middle of a pandemic during the lockdown, so he could begin renovations to start his new school using PLG funding. The story will also include other voices who have been at the short end of the PLG story.
